title: Canada Is Spending $500 Billion on Defence. It Wants India to Help Build the Arsenal.
excerpt: From expelled diplomats to a full defence dialogue in four months — Canada and India are engineering one of the fastest diplomatic turnarounds in recent memory, with a free trade deal and a Modi visit to Ottawa on the horizon.
body:
A year ago, India and Canada could barely manage a civil phone call. Their top diplomats had been expelled, intelligence accusations hung in the air, and the very idea of defence cooperation between Ottawa and New Delhi would have drawn blank stares in both capitals.

Today, Canada's High Commissioner to India is talking about a "$500 billion hockey stick" in defence spending and actively courting Indian companies to build weapons together. The transformation is among the most dramatic diplomatic pivots either country has executed in decades — and it carries enormous implications for the nearly two million Indians and people of Indian origin who call Canada home.

The Hockey Stick

High Commissioner Chris Cooter's description of Canada's defence spending trajectory is neither casual nor metaphorical. Having crossed NATO's 2% of GDP threshold, Canada is now on a fast track toward 5% — a commitment that, for the world's ninth-largest economy, translates into roughly $500 billion in additional military spending by 2035.

"We have lots of advanced technology, but we don't have the scale, we don't have the market," Cooter said. The arithmetic is straightforward: Canada needs manufacturing capacity to match its spending ambitions, and India has precisely that.

The opening is deliberate. Since Prime Minister Mark Carney replaced Justin Trudeau and flew to New Delhi in March for a reset meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the two governments have moved at a pace that has surprised even their own bureaucracies.

https://www.instagram.com/reel/DVWsC9TkiC9/

What's Actually Happening

The list of deliverables is no longer aspirational. In less than four months, India and Canada have:

  • Launched an **India-Canada Defence Dialogue**, the first institutionalised military-to-military channel between the two countries

> "Today, Canada's High Commissioner to India is talking about a "$500 billion hockey stick" in defence spending and actively courting Indian companies to build weapons together."

  • Begun negotiations on a **General Security of Information Agreement** (GSOIA) — the legal framework that allows companies from both countries to handle classified defence information and pursue joint ventures
  • Appointed a Canadian **Defence Attaché to India** for the first time, with India reciprocally accrediting its Washington-based Defence Attaché to Ottawa
  • Established a new **maritime security partnership** covering defence material cooperation, supply chain resilience, and joint training
  • Launched the **Canada-India Trade and Investment Forum**, with Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal leading India's largest-ever business delegation to Canada
  • Set a target to conclude the **Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement** (CEPA) — a full free trade deal — by the end of 2026

![New Delhi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg/3840px-Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg)

At the recent CANSEC conference, Canada's largest defence industry gathering, attendance surged and Indian participation was conspicuously higher than in previous years.

Beyond Guns and Ships

The partnership extends into territory that directly touches the diaspora. Cooter highlighted two areas of security collaboration that affect Indians on both sides of the Pacific: combating fentanyl precursors, where the chemical supply chain runs through both countries, and dismantling international scam centres that exploit citizens in India and Canada alike.

"We've progressed now in that security dialogue to manage the bilateral irritants more effectively, but also to look beyond to see where we can cooperate on a regional or a global basis," Cooter said.

Canada's Foreign Minister Anita Anand, in her own remarks following talks with External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, underscored that the security dialogue would continue alongside elevated cooperation in critical minerals, energy, AI and climate.

Jaishankar, for his part, framed the relationship in structural terms. "When we look at Canada, we see a complementary economy, another open society, and a partner that shares India's values of diversity and pluralism," he said.

Modi to Visit Canada

The diplomatic choreography has one more major act: Prime Minister Modi has been invited to visit Canada later this year. On the sidelines of the G7 Summit in Evian, Modi and Carney held what the Indian PM called their fourth meeting in less than a year — "indicating our commitment to strong India-Canada ties."

Both sides are finalising dates through diplomatic channels. A Modi visit to Canada would be the most visible symbol yet that the Trudeau-era frost is not just thawing but has been replaced by something substantially warmer.

The establishment of Raisina Americas — a new platform for dialogue, exchanges and cooperation — signals that both governments see this as a long-term strategic realignment, not a temporary diplomatic convenience.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian-Canadian community, the thaw is personal. Years of diplomatic tension had chilled everything from visa processing to business investment to the simple comfort of knowing your two countries were on speaking terms.

The defence partnership, in particular, opens a new economic corridor. Canadian defence firms looking for manufacturing scale will need Indian partners, and Indian aerospace and defence companies eyeing Western markets will need Canadian entry points. The CEPA, if concluded, would be India's first comprehensive trade deal with a G7 economy other than the UK agreement taking effect this month.

Canada is also planning a "Team Canada Trade Mission" to India later this year, and India has backed Canada's bid to join the Indian Ocean Rim Association as a Dialogue Partner — a gesture that carries strategic weight in the Indo-Pacific.

The question now is whether the institutional architecture being built can survive the inevitable political turbulences ahead. For the moment, both capitals appear to have decided that the cost of estrangement was higher than anyone anticipated — and that making up for lost time requires moving fast.
